transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is the historical society project. I just... I took it on like I could run the entire fundraiser all by myself. Which is funny because I remember when Mary—she used to be the president—ran it back in 2018, she had a committee of six people. Mary moved to Florida, though. Tampa, I think? Or maybe Naples, she always liked the Gulf side better because the water is warmer and she has that arthritis in her knees. 

Anyway, I started drafting all these new quilt designs for the auction. Quilting is such a lost art, my grandmother taught me when I was nine on this heavy old cast-iron Singer sewing machine with the foot pedal. You just don't see craftsmanship like that anymore, everything is so mass-produced now! But yes, I was calling all the volunteers, drafting up these massive schedules, and just... promising deadlines I couldn't possibly meet. It all just sort of snowballed.
Do you often find yourself getting stuck on certain ideas or tasks, like the quilt designs for the auction?

I suppose I do. Actually, my husband was just saying something about that to me. He said I went from pacing around the sewing room, just sorting the exact same fabric piles over and over again... I have a lot of calico prints, you see. I get them from this wonderful little shop in Lancaster. Have you ever been out to Amish country? Oh, it's just lovely in the fall. We went there for our 25th anniversary and had the most incredible shoofly pie. It's so sweet it practically makes your teeth ache, but you just can't stop eating it. 

But yes, my husband said I went from pacing and sorting nonstop like that to... well, to moving so slowly some mornings that even making coffee feels like a chore. And we just use a standard Mr. Coffee machine, nothing complicated! My daughter keeps telling me to buy one of those Keurigs because it's supposed to be easier, but I just can't stand the thought of all those little plastic pods sitting in a landfill forever. The environmental impact of those things is just devastating when you really look into it, don't you think? 

Wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, getting stuck on the designs... yes, I suppose the fabric sorting was a bit like that.
Do you often feel guilty about things that happen or decisions you make?

Guilty? Oh... yes. Constantly. I just keep going over every single late order for those quilts, and... and every sharp thing I said to the volunteers when I was trying to get the schedules together. I just sit there telling myself I completely let the church down, and the historical society, and really this whole town. 

The church has been so good to us, too. Pastor Thomas actually just had his hip replaced last month, and I feel awful I haven't brought him a casserole yet. It's a marvel what they can do with surgery these days, isn't it? They had him up and walking the very next afternoon! My uncle Henry had a hip replacement back in the eighties and he was in the hospital for weeks. Uncle Henry was a carpenter, he made the most beautiful cedar chests. He made one for my hope chest when I was sixteen. Cedar smells so wonderful, and it keeps the moths away from the wool sweaters. I have this lovely thick Irish wool sweater I bought in Galway... or was it Dublin? No, it was definitely Galway, because it rained the entire time we were on the coast and we had to duck into this tiny little shop near the docks to stay dry, and the woman working there made us tea... 

I'm sorry, I completely lost my train of thought again. Were we talking about the church volunteers?
Do you often have thoughts that repeat over and over in your mind and feel like you can't stop them?

Repeating thoughts? I... I don't really think so. Not like a broken record or anything. Though speaking of records, my husband just bought this new turntable. He's been getting back into vinyl, which is so popular again, isn't it? He found this old Fleetwood Mac album at a garage sale last weekend. "Rumours," I think it was. Such a classic! The woman running the sale said she was clearing out her father's attic. Attics can just get so cluttered, can't they? We have boxes up in ours that haven't been opened since we moved in back in '98. I keep meaning to go through them, especially the old photo albums. My daughter wants to scan them all onto the computer so we don't lose them if there's ever a fire. Fire is just such a terrifying thought, especially with all these dry spells we've been having. The grass in the front yard is completely brown. I tried watering it, but there's a restriction in the town right now... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the thoughts. No, I don't really have thoughts repeating like that. Just... just the guilt about the quilts, really.
Do you feel a strong need to perform certain routines or rituals in a specific way?

Routines? Rituals? No, I wouldn't say I have anything like that. I mean, I like things to be orderly, but I don't have to do them a certain way every single time. Although, speaking of doing things a certain way, my neighbor Susan across the street is just fastidious about her gardening. She's out there every morning at exactly 7:00 AM, rain or shine, pruning her rose bushes. She has these beautiful yellow roses—Peace roses, I think they're called. They smell absolutely heavenly. My grandmother used to grow roses, but hers were always red. She had this huge trellis in her backyard that was just covered in them. We used to play hide-and-seek behind it when I was a little girl. My brother was always the best at hiding, he was so skinny he could fit behind the rain barrel without anyone seeing him. He lives in Florida now, actually. Works in real estate. The market down there is just booming, he says, though I don't know how anyone can stand the humidity. I went to visit him last August and I felt like I was breathing soup the whole time. Plus, the mosquitoes are the size of small birds! 

I'm sorry, I'm rambling again, aren't I? What was the question? Something about routines? No, I don't really have any strict routines I have to follow.
Do you often feel restless or have trouble sitting still?

Restless? Well, it really depends on when you ask. My husband, he actually just mentioned this the other day. He says I went from pacing around the sewing room, just sorting the same piles of fabric over and over... I had this beautiful stack of calico prints I got at a craft fair in Vermont. We went up there to see the leaves change, you know, the foliage is just breathtaking in October. The reds and golds... we stayed at this charming little bed and breakfast run by a couple who used to live in the city but gave it all up to make maple syrup. Real maple syrup, not that high-fructose stuff you get at the grocery store. We bought three jugs of it to bring home, and I gave one to my sister, but she said it was too sweet for her. I don't know how syrup can be too sweet, it's syrup! She's always been picky, though, even when we were kids. She would only eat the crusts off the bread if they were cut into triangles. 

Anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, my husband. Yes, he said I went from pacing and sorting fabric like a madwoman to... well, lately, moving so slowly some mornings that even making a pot of coffee feels like a monumental chore. Just dragging myself around the kitchen.
Do you feel like you have to check things multiple times to make sure they're done correctly?

Checking things multiple times? No, I don't think I do that. I mean, I'll make sure the front door is locked before bed, but just the once. My husband usually handles the doors anyway. He's always been very particular about the locks ever since we had that string of car break-ins in the neighborhood back in... oh, it must have been 2012. Or maybe 2013? It was right around the time they repaved Elm Street. They took weeks to finish that road, just left the orange cones everywhere and dug up all the asphalt. It was an absolute nightmare trying to get to the grocery store. I had to take the long way around past the old high school. 

They tore that school down recently, you know. Built a whole new complex with a fancy football stadium. The property taxes went up something awful because of it. We were actually talking about maybe downsizing to a condo to save money, but I just can't imagine giving up my sewing room. It has the best natural light in the mornings, right when the sun comes up over the oak trees in the backyard. The squirrels out there are getting so bold, though, they come right up to the window screen...

I'm doing it again, aren't I? Losing my train of thought completely. What did you ask me about? Oh, checking things. Right. No, I don't have any problem with having to check things over and over. Once is usually enough for me.
Do you often find yourself being overly critical of yourself when things don't go as planned?

Critical of myself? Oh... yes. Lately, it's just been awful. I just keep going over every little thing. Like the bake sale last month... I keep thinking about every late order, every sharp thing I said to the volunteers. I just keep telling myself I let the church down, the historical society, this whole town, really. 

The historical society used to be so vibrant, you know. Back when Mrs. Gable was running it. She had this incredible collection of antique thimbles. Hundreds of them, from all over the world. Some were silver, some porcelain, hand-painted with tiny little roses... just exquisite. She kept them in this beautiful glass display case that her grandfather built. He was a carpenter, came over from Germany in the twenties. They don't make furniture like that anymore, do they? Now it's all just particle board and Allen wrenches. We bought a bookshelf from one of those big box stores last year and my husband nearly threw his back out trying to put it together. He was cursing a blue streak, and the dog got so scared she hid under the sofa for three hours. She's a rescue, part beagle, part goodness-knows-what, but she's got the sweetest eyes. 

Oh dear... I've wandered off again. What were we talking about? Being critical? Yes... I just feel so guilty about everything lately, like I ruin everything I touch.
Do you feel like your guilt over things like the quilts and the bake sale is disproportionate to what actually happened?

Disproportionate? Well... I don't know if it's disproportionate. It feels very real to me. I just... I keep going over every late order in my head, and every sharp thing I said to the volunteers. I just keep telling myself I let the church down, the historical society, and honestly, this whole town. 

The town really relies on that bake sale, you know. We use the funds to keep the old library roof from leaking. It's a slate roof, original to the building from 1894. You can't just get anyone to fix a slate roof these days, you have to find a specialist. We had a fellow come down from Portland a few years ago to look at it, and he charged us an arm and a leg just for the estimate. Portland is getting so expensive, though. My niece lives up there, she rents a tiny little apartment that costs more than our mortgage ever did. She works in marketing, or maybe public relations? Something with computers. She's always on her phone, even at Thanksgiving dinner. It drives my husband crazy, he thinks it's so disrespectful. He actually instituted a "no phones at the table" rule last year, which meant we actually had to talk to each other. We ended up having a lovely conversation about... oh, what was it? Bird watching, I think. We had a pair of cardinals nesting in the lilac bush...

Oh, I'm so sorry. I'm rambling again, aren't I? But yes, the guilt... I just feel like I've let everyone down so terribly.
Do you often feel guilty about things beyond just the historical society project and the bake sale?

Beyond just those two things? Oh, well... yes, I suppose I do. It just feels like everything I touch lately turns out wrong. I just keep going over every single late order from that bake sale, and every sharp thing I said to the poor volunteers who were just trying to help. I just keep telling myself I let the church down, the historical society, and really, this whole town. 

The town isn't what it used to be, though. The downtown area used to be so bustling on a Saturday morning. You couldn't find a parking spot on Main Street if your life depended on it. Now half the storefronts are empty. They opened up that big shopping center out on Route 9, and it just pulled everyone away. My husband says it's progress, but I don't see what's progressive about a giant concrete parking lot. We used to have a lovely little hardware store right on the corner, run by Mr. Henderson. He always had a jar of butterscotch candies on the counter for the kids. My son used to love those. He's grown now, of course, living out in Denver. He sent us a picture of the snow they got last week, it was up to his knees! I don't know how people live in that kind of cold, my joints would just seize right up. I have enough trouble with my knees when it rains here...

Oh dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I just can't seem to keep my thoughts straight today. But yes, the guilt is just... it's heavy. I just feel like I've failed everyone.
Do you ever feel an overwhelming urge to repeat certain actions or behaviors?

Repeat things? Like doing something over and over? No... no, I don't think I experience anything like that. Not like my old neighbor, Mrs. Higgins. She used to sweep her front walk three times a day, regular as clockwork. She had this beautiful brick pathway leading up to her house, the old-fashioned kind with the herringbone pattern. You don't see craftsmanship like that much anymore. Everyone just pours concrete now. 

My husband wanted to pour a concrete patio in our backyard last spring, but I told him it would completely ruin the look of the garden. We have these gorgeous hydrangeas back there. The soil here is so acidic, they turn the most brilliant shade of blue. I tried cutting some to bring inside last week, but I couldn't find my good pruning shears. I think my husband borrowed them to open a package and never put them back. He's always doing that with my gardening tools, just taking them and leaving them in the garage. The garage is an absolute disaster area, honestly. You can barely fit the car in there with all the boxes of old vinyl records he refuses to part with. He insists they're going to be worth money someday, but who even owns a record player anymore? Well, I suppose the young people are getting back into them. Everything old is new again, isn't it? 

Oh, goodness... I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? You were asking about repeating actions? No, I don't get any urges like that. Just the guilt, really.
Do you often feel guilty about things that have nothing to do with the historical society or your relationships with others?

Other things? Well, I try to think about other things, but my mind just gets stuck on the same loop. I know I keep bringing it up, and I know you just asked about other things, but it's just consuming me. I just keep going over every late order in my head, and every sharp thing I said to the volunteers. I just can't stop telling myself that I let the church down, the historical society, and honestly, this whole town. 

Especially how I spoke to Susan during the rush. She was just trying to help with the cashbox. She always volunteers for the cashbox because she used to be a bank teller down at the First National. Well, that was before they got bought out by that big conglomerate and changed all the signs to that awful bright green. I never liked the green. The old signs were a lovely navy blue, very dignified. My father always said you should only trust a bank with blue signage. He was a very particular man, my father. He wore a suit and tie every single day, even on Sundays just to sit in his armchair and read the paper. You really don't see men dressing like that anymore, do you? Now it's all sweatpants and those rubber shoes with the holes in them... Crocs, I think they're called? They look exactly like gardening shoes to me. I would never wear them to the grocery store, but you see people in them everywhere now. 

Anyway... I'm so sorry, my mind is just wandering all over the place again. But to answer your question, no, it always comes back to the same thing. Just that terrible feeling that I've let the church and the town down. It just won't stop playing in my head.
Do you feel guilty about things that happen in your daily life at home, not just related to the historical society or volunteer work?

Well, at home... I mean, I try to focus on the house, on my husband, but I just... I can't seem to separate it. It always comes back to the same thing. I know we've talked about it, but I just keep going over every single late order from that bake sale. Every sharp, awful thing I said to the volunteers... I just sit in my living room and tell myself I let the church down, the historical society, the whole town. 

Speaking of the living room, my husband finally agreed to let me change the drapes. We've had these heavy velvet ones since we moved in, and they just gather so much dust. Dusting is such a chore, isn't it? My mother used to have this special feather duster made of real ostrich feathers. She ordered it from a catalog back in the seventies. Catalogs used to be so wonderful. You'd get the big Sears Roebuck one right before Christmas, and it was thick as a phone book. Kids today don't even know what a phone book is, do they? They just look everything up on those little screens. My nephew was over last Thanksgiving, and he didn't look up from his phone the entire meal. I made my special cranberry sauce, the one with the orange zest, and I don't even think he tasted it. It's a shame, really, people don't appreciate a good home-cooked meal anymore. 

Oh, listen to me rambling again. I'm sorry, doctor. But yes, even at home, the guilt is just... it's always there, about the volunteers and the church. I just can't shake it.
Do you feel like your guilt is affecting your relationships with your family?

Well, my husband... yes, it's really taken a toll on him. He's had to take over basically all the household routines, the cooking, the cleaning. I just stopped keeping any of my commitments. I couldn't even face going down to the historical society anymore, so he's been dealing with them, too. I just couldn't face the people waiting on me, knowing how badly I failed them. 

He's been so patient, though. He even went down to the hardware store to get the right kind of lightbulbs for the hallway. We have those old fixtures, you know, the brass ones that take the little candelabra bulbs. They're so hard to find these days. Everything is LED now. They say it saves energy, but the light is just so harsh and blue. It makes everything look like a hospital waiting room. I remember when we first bought the house, all the lights had this warm, yellow glow. It felt so cozy, especially in the winter when it gets dark by 4:30. The winters here seem to be getting longer, don't they? Or maybe I'm just noticing it more now that I don't go out as much. I used to love the snow, building snowmen with the kids when they were little. We had this old carrot nose that we kept in the freezer year-round, just for the snowmen. 

Oh, dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry. But yes, my husband has had to do everything because I just... I can't face anyone right now.
Are you having trouble completing your usual daily tasks at home because of your guilt?

Well, yes, I suppose I am having trouble. Like I was saying, I just stopped keeping my commitments. I couldn't face the people waiting on me, so my husband has had to take over all the household routines. He even deals with the historical society for me now. 

He's always been good at dealing with people, though. He used to be in sales, you know. Sold encyclopedias door-to-door when we were first married. People don't do that anymore. Now you just look everything up on the internet. But there was something so nice about having that big set of books on the shelf. The bindings were a beautiful maroon color, with gold lettering on the spine. They looked so smart in the den. We had this oak bookcase that my grandfather built... he was a carpenter, my grandfather. He could build anything with his own two hands. He built a cedar chest for my grandmother for their wedding, and it still smells like fresh cedar when you open it. I keep all our winter blankets in there. The heavy wool ones. Wool is so itchy, though, isn't it? I prefer a nice cotton quilt. 

Oh, I'm sorry, I'm wandering off again. But yes, my husband is doing everything at home because I just can't seem to manage it right now.
Are you finding it difficult to enjoy activities you used to like because of your guilt?

Well, yes... I suppose that's true, too. I used to love checking my garden every morning, and I was always working on my own quilt entries for the county fair. But lately... I just look at the fabric and the seed catalogs and I feel nothing much at all. It's just empty. 

Speaking of the fair, they really changed the layout last year. They moved the agriculture exhibits all the way to the south end of the fairgrounds, right next to the midway. The noise from those rides is just awful. You're trying to look at the prize-winning pumpkins and all you hear is that terrible mechanical screaming from the Tilt-A-Whirl. My kids used to love the Tilt-A-Whirl. They'd ride it until they were green in the face. Then they'd want cotton candy, which I always thought was a terrible idea, sugar on top of all that spinning. Cotton candy is just spun sugar and food coloring, really. It gets everywhere. Your hands get sticky, your face gets sticky... I remember trying to get that pink dye out of my daughter's favorite white blouse. I soaked it in lemon juice and baking soda for two days. Lemon juice is wonderful for stains, you know. My grandmother swore by it. She used to clean the brass doorknobs with lemon and salt... 

Oh, goodness, I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm doing it again. But yes, I just don't have any interest in the gardening or the quilting right now. I just can't seem to care about them.
Have you been having trouble sleeping because of your guilt?

Well, yes, my sleep has been all over the place. For a while there, I was only sleeping a few hours a night, but I'd wake up just buzzing, ready to sew or make phone calls at three in the morning. I even called my sister in Ohio once before the sun was up. She was terrified, thought someone had died. We haven't been as close since she moved out there. Ohio is so flat, isn't it? I drove through it once on the way to a quilt show in Indiana. Just miles and miles of cornfields. It's beautiful in its own way, I suppose, but I missed the hills we have around here. The leaves are turning so early this year, have you noticed? The maples down our street are already dropping their leaves, and it's barely even autumn. I usually have my husband rake them, but he's been so busy taking over everything else... 

Anyway, now it's completely different. Now I either lie awake for hours, just staring at the ceiling and worrying about everything I've ruined, or I sleep late into the morning and still feel completely worn out. It's like I can't win either way.
Do you feel like your guilt is consistently affecting how you interact with your family and friends?

Well, yes, I suppose it is. I just... I can't look anyone in the eye anymore. I keep going over every late order for the quilt show and every sharp thing I said to the volunteers when I was... well, when I was feeling so wound up before. I keep telling myself I let the church down, and the historical society, and really this whole town. 

The historical society used to meet in the old library basement, you know. It smelled like old paper and damp stone down there. We had this terrible water leak back in '98, ruined half the town records from the 1800s. The mayor was furious. He was a very red-faced man, Mayor Higgins. He always wore these awful plaid suits that his wife bought him from a catalog. I don't think she liked him very much, honestly. She spent most of her time at the country club playing bridge. I tried to learn bridge once, but the rules are just so complicated. All that bidding and trumping. I prefer a simple game of gin rummy. My husband and I used to play gin rummy on the porch during thunderstorms... 

Oh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry. But yes, I just feel like I've ruined everything with everyone, so I just stay away.
Do you feel like your guilt is always affecting how you interact with your family and friends?

Well, yes, I suppose I just said that, didn't I? It's just... it's all falling apart, and my poor husband is bearing the brunt of it. He's had to take over all the household routines, the cooking, the cleaning, even paying the bills. He's terrible with the checkbook, honestly. He always forgets to carry the one when he subtracts, and then the bank calls... The tellers at our bank are so young now. I swear they look like they're still in high school. When I was a girl, working at the bank was a career. You wore a nice suit and you knew everyone's name. I had a lovely navy blue suit with a matching pillbox hat. Very Jackie Kennedy. She had such wonderful style, didn't she? Always so put together, even when things were so awful for her. I read a biography about her once, or maybe it was an article in a magazine... 

But anyway, my husband, he's even had to deal with the historical society for me. I just stopped going to meetings, stopped keeping my commitments. I couldn't face them, not with all those people waiting on me and me feeling so... so wretched about how I let them down before. So he has to go and make excuses for me. It's not fair to him, it really isn't.
Has your guilt been affecting your interactions with family and friends for a long time now?

Well, it feels like forever, to be honest. Since the orders for the quilt show fell behind and all those awful conflicts with the volunteers blew up... I've been stuck in this terrible, low, guilty place for about nine months now. Nine months. That's how long it takes to have a baby, isn't it? I remember when I was pregnant with my first, I was so sick for the first trimester. Just couldn't keep anything down except saltines and ginger ale. My mother used to bring me ginger ale from the corner store. It was that little shop owned by Mr. Henderson. He always wore a bowtie, every single day. Even in the dead of summer when it was sweltering out. They don't make men like that anymore, do they? People are so casual now. You go to the grocery store and people are wearing their pajama pants! I just can't understand it. I was raised that you always put your best foot forward when you leave the house. You never know who you might run into... 

But yes, nine whole months of feeling like this. Just dragging myself through the days and hiding from everyone because of what I did.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about obsessive thoughts (thoughts that repeat over and over and cannot be stopped), which is a screening question for OCD. The patient's profile does not include obsessions. While the patient has Racing Thoughts (S038) and Worthlessness/Guilt (S030), neither matches the specific definition of repetitive, unstoppable obsessive thoughts.
